report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is not supported by high-quality evidence. Studies evaluating relevant measures of childhood vaccine exposure—including cumulative immune-stimulating components and aluminum-adjuvanted vaccine exposure—have found no increased autism risk. A large nationwide Danish cohort of more than 1.2 million children found no association between aluminum exposure from early-childhood vaccines and neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism. WHO’s vaccine-safety committee likewise concludes there is no evidence that MMR causes autism.

Autism can become noticeable during the same early-childhood period when many vaccinations are scheduled; timing alone does not establish causation. The evidence does not support reducing or delaying recommended vaccines as a way to prevent autism, while doing so can leave children vulnerable to serious infections.

Sources:  
- World Health Organization, “MMR vaccines and autism”: https://www.who.int/groups/global-advisory-committee-on-vaccine-safety/topics/mmr-vaccines-and-autism  
- JAMA, nationwide Danish cohort: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2837599  
- PubMed record, *Aluminum-Adsorbed Vaccines and Chronic Diseases in Childhood*: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40658954/  
- Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, “Vaccines Do Not Cause Autism”: https://publichealth.jhu.edu/2025/vaccines-do-not-cause-autism
